- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

"""Offline autonomous node coordination baseline."""

__version__ = "0.1.0"

content.content:
1	# Offline Autonomous Node Coordination
2	
3	Minimal backend baseline for autonomous nodes that must keep working during long network outages and later reconcile state with explainable rules.
4	
5	Requires Python 3.11 or newer and has no third-party runtime dependencies.
6	
7	```bash
8	python -m offline_coordination status
9	python -m offline_coordination recovery check LEDGER [LEDGER ...]
10	python -m offline_coordination recovery run LEDGER [LEDGER ...] --keyring KEYRING --ticket TICKET --moment MOMENT --audit AUDIT
11	python -m offline_coordination recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]
12	python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
13	```
14	
15	The baseline exposes a local status command plus offline ledger recovery operations. Persistent state is available via `offline_coordination.storage` and an append-only hash-chained audit log via `offline_coordination.audit`. Replication, conflict policies, security boundaries, observability, and network services are intentionally left for subsequent tasks.
16	
17	## Ledger recovery
18	
19	`offline_coordination.replication.recover_ledger(path)` settles one interrupted ledger transaction. Its `clean` result (no recovery intent) reports the SHA-256 of the current ledger bytes, lowercase hex, or `None` when the path is missing.
20	
21	Two batch entry points operate on an explicit, non-empty list of distinct, non-empty ledger paths, validated in full before any file is read or modified (`TypeError` for container/element type faults, `ValueError` for an empty list, empty path or duplicate):
22	
23	- `inspect_recovery(paths)` — read-only diagnostics. Each report carries `path`, `status`, `phase`, `digest`, `artifacts`, `action` and `error`: `clean` when no intent exists, `pending` with the suggested action (`rollback`/`complete`) and candidate/predecessor existence, digest-match and completeness when an intent is valid, `blocked`/`corrupt` when the intent or a necessary artifact is invalid, and `failed`/`os-error` when reading fails. Nothing is created, modified or deleted, and random artifacts are never scanned.
24	- `recover_many(paths)` — controlled batch recovery. Each ledger is recovered via `recover_ledger` in order; one failure never stops or rolls back the others. Successful items keep the `clean`/`rolled-back`/`completed` statuses; a `CorruptRecoveryError` becomes a `blocked`/`corrupt` item and an `OSError` a `failed`/`os-error` item, leaving enough intent and artifacts behind for an independent retry.
25	
26	The module entry points `recovery check` and `recovery run` wrap these: they print exactly one line of compact UTF-8 JSON with recursively sorted keys, exit 0 when every ledger succeeds, 1 when any ledger is blocked or failed, and 2 on syntax or argument errors.
27	
28	## Authorized recovery and the recovery audit
29	
30	`offline_coordination.replication.recover_authorized(paths, keyring, ticket, moment, audit)` adds an authorization boundary and a durable operation audit around the same batch recovery. The ticket is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline, space or any other byte after the closing brace; it carries exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload carries exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `nonce`, `notBefore`, `notAfter` and the ordered `paths`, and the signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload encoding, verified against the keyring (the same version/secret/validity/revocation rules as `apply_signed_remote`, keys selected by exact issuer and version). The command paths must equal the ticket paths item for item — never expanded, reordered or normalized. Unknown credentials, a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key or ticket, a path mismatch and a signature mismatch all raise `AuthenticationError` before any ledger is read, so a failed authorization creates no audit record, consumes no nonce and leaves no temporary file. An old-style ticket carrying a trailing newline (or any other non-canonical encoding) raises `ValueError`; field type faults raise `TypeError` (a `bool` never poses as `moment`); a malformed ticket key set, nonce, validity interval or signature format raises `ValueError`.
31	
32	Once authorized, the batch runs in the `recover_many` order with the same per-ledger isolation and the same public item structure, and every step is recorded at the audit path as an append-only canonical JSONL hash chain, each record written, flushed and synced before the step it gates: a `batch` header on the first use of a nonce (binding the ticket digest, issuer and ordered paths), then a `before` record (original digest, phase, planned action) and an `after` record (new digest, status, failure category) per ledger. An `OSError` while reading the audit or writing, flushing or syncing a record propagates unchanged and leaves a consistent, retryable chain prefix. Re-entering with the same nonce and the same ticket reuses the recorded results and only continues the paths not yet settled — a process interrupted after a recovery but before its result record is completed from the recorded action and digests, without repeating side effects. The same nonce bound to a different ticket raises `ReplayError` (a `ValueError`) without modifying any file; a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError` (a `ValueError`).
33	
34	`export_recovery_audit(path, after=0, limit=100)` pages the chain read-only (`after`/`complete`/`next`/`records`), validating the whole chain and treating a missing audit as an empty chain. The module entry point `recovery run` requires the four explicit materials `--keyring`, `--ticket`, `--moment` and `--audit` and exits 0 on success, 1 on ledger failures and 2 on authorization or argument errors; `recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]` prints one page of the chain.
35	
36	`export_recovery_checkpoint(audit, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` adds an offline signature anchor that a later full-history replacement cannot recompute. It reads and validates the whole chain read-only and returns `bytes`: one compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline or any other trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`. The payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `lastSeq`, `moment`, `tail` and `version` (integer 1) — `lastSeq` is the last chain seq (0 for a missing audit) and `tail` the last record hash (the zero hash for an empty chain). `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key the keyring binds to the exact issuer and version, with no fallback; unknown credentials and a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key raise `AuthenticationError`, a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError`, and an `OSError` while reading propagates unchanged.
37	
38	`verify_recovery_page(checkpoint, page, keyring, moment, cursor=None)` verifies a page dict against the checkpoint entirely offline — no file is read and no argument is modified. The checkpoint is parsed and its HMAC verified against the current keyring (exact issuer/version, usable at `moment`, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it); the bound `moment` is part of the signed payload itself. The first call passes no cursor and the page's `after` must be zero; later calls pass `{"digest", "next", "tail"}` built from the previous result, so `after` must equal the cursor `next`, the first record must chain to the cursor `tail`, and the cursor `digest` must equal this checkpoint's SHA-256 digest — a cursor can never resume another checkpoint. Each page's records must be contiguous from `after + 1` (no empty page, gap, reordering, duplicate or predecessor mismatch before the signed end), hash-correct within the page and across the paging boundary, and verification never crosses the signed `lastSeq`. The result carries `digest`, `lastSeq`, `status` and `tail`: reaching the signed tail is `verified`, every earlier page `continue`. An empty checkpoint accepts only an empty page starting at zero and directly reports seq 0, the zero hash and `verified`. Parameter or field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); keyring structure or format faults raise `ValueError`; checkpoint faults raise `InvalidRecoveryCheckpointError` and page or cursor faults raise `InvalidRecoveryPageError`, both `ValueError` subclasses.
39	
40	`verify_recovery_checkpoints(items, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of checkpoints offline and never reads a file. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id`, the `checkpoint` bytes and the non-empty `pages` list holding that checkpoint's paging dicts in export order. The batch is validated in full before any item is verified — container, field or element type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id, a wrong item key set or an empty page list raises `ValueError` (keyring and `moment`, a non-negative non-bool int, keep their usual classification). Each item is then handled in input order and in isolation: its pages are walked from a zero cursor through the exact `verify_recovery_page` rules, each cursor bound to the same checkpoint digest and the previous page's chain tail; keys are selected by the checkpoint's own exact issuer and version with no fallback, so checkpoints signed before and after a key rotation verify independently in one batch while the keyring retains both versions. Pages that reach the signed `lastSeq` must end there (any further page is a page fault); pages exhausted earlier are `incomplete` and keep the verified boundary. The result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items`, `version` (integer 1); each item report carries `id`, the checkpoint `digest`, the signed `issuer` and `keyVersion` (both null when the checkpoint does not parse), the verified `boundary` (`{"lastSeq","tail"}`, null when nothing was verified), a `status` of `verified`, `incomplete`, `invalid-checkpoint`, `invalid-page` or `unauthenticated`, and an `error` message (null exactly when verified). Only a batch-level or keyring-level fault raises — one item's failure never stops the later items, and no input is modified.
41	
42	`adjudicate_recovery(items, policy, keyring, moment)` aggregates those per-site verifications into one offline verdict, reading no file and modifying no input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and `attestation` bytes. An attestation is a compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `site`, `keyVersion` and `result` with no extra fields, where `result` has the single-item batch verification shape (`boundary`, `digest`, `error`, `id`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `status`). Every legal single-item result is accepted: a `verified` result always carries identity, a positive key version and a boundary, while a non-verified result may carry a null issuer/keyVersion (when the checkpoint did not parse) or a null boundary — its identity, digest, boundary and status are preserved — and only a `verified` result may count. `policy` is `{"batch", "sites", "threshold"}`: the authorized batch id, a positive threshold no greater than the site count, and a non-empty map of each authorized site to its non-empty set of allowed positive key versions; `keyring` and `moment` keep their existing structure, validity and revocation rules. The signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key selected by the exact site and version, with no fallback.
43	
44	A batch or identity that is not authorized, unavailable/revoked/not-yet-valid/expired credentials, a wrong signature or a non-verified result each reject the packet with a fixed reason (`unauthorized-batch`, `unauthorized-site`, `unauthorized-version`, `credential-unavailable`, `revoked`, `not-yet-valid`, `expired`, `bad-signature`, `not-verified`) and never count; one packet with illegal encoding, key sets or fields is rejected alone as `invalid-attestation` without blocking the others. For one site an identical valid packet — the complete embedded result equal on every field — counts once and extra copies are `duplicate`; any different valid result (even one sharing digest and boundary) is a self-`contradiction`. Valid packets from different sites must agree on both digest and boundary — any disagreement is a fork a majority cannot outvote. The return is one canonical compact JSON object with the top-level keys `boundary`, `digest`, `items`, `status`, `threshold` and `version` (integer 1), no trailing byte: any contradiction or cross-site fork is `conflicted` with a null digest and boundary; a unique agreed result attested by at least the threshold of distinct sites is `accepted`; everything else is `insufficient`. Every packet stays in `items` — sorted stably by site then id — with its identity, conclusion (`valid`/`invalid`/`duplicate`/`contradiction`), fixed reason (null only for valid) and boundary, and the verdict does not depend on input order. Parameter, container or public field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an empty list, duplicate id or illegal threshold, site or version rule raises `ValueError`.
45	
46	`export_recovery_verdict(verdict, policy, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` signs that aggregate verdict for offline handover, reading and writing no file. It takes the canonical compact verdict bytes `adjudicate_recovery` returned, the same policy, a keyring, the signing issuer, key version and moment. It returns one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest` and the complete `verdict`. The policy is canonicalized — sites in ascending order and each site's versions as an ascending array, all keys recursively sorted into compact UTF-8 — and `policyDigest` is its SHA-256; `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback. Unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`. A non-bytes verdict or a wrong field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); a bad issuer, version or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal verdict raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictError`.
47	
48	`verify_recovery_verdict(proof, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies such a handover proof entirely offline from just the proof, the policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It recomputes the two digests, checks the batch, threshold, signing moment, proof/verdict structure and digest bindings, and re-checks the credentials against the current keyring (exact issuer/version usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it). It returns a fresh dict keyed `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest`, `verdictDigest`, `status`, `digest`, `boundary`, `items` and `version` (integer 1). A non-bytes proof or a wrong public field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an illegal policy, identifier, version or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal verdict argument to `export_recovery_verdict` raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictError`, while a bad proof structure — including an illegal verdict structure, field type or canonical encoding bound into the payload — a digest mismatch or a batch/threshold binding fault raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictProofError` (both subclass `ValueError`); a bad signature or current credentials raise `AuthenticationError`.
49	
50	`verify_recovery_verdicts(items, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of those handover proofs offline and never reads or writes a file or modifies an input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and the `proof` bytes. The batch is validated in full — container, element or public field type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or a wrong item key set raises `ValueError` — together with the shared `policy`, `keyring` and `moment`, which keep the single-entry validation and exception classification (a non-negative non-bool int) before any proof is verified; only such a batch-level fault raises. Each item is then verified independently, in strict input order, through the exact `verify_recovery_verdict` rules: one proof's failure never stops a later item or changes an earlier report, and each proof selects its key by its own exact issuer and key version with no fallback, so proofs bound to different issuers or rotations coexist in one batch. A currently revoked, not-yet-valid, expired or missing credential or a wrong signature makes that item `unauthenticated`; an illegal encoding, key set, field, digest, batch, threshold, signing moment or embedded verdict makes it `invalid-proof`; a passing proof is `verified`. The top-level result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items` and `version` (integer 1); each item report has the fixed key order `error`, `id`, `result`, `status`, where a verified item keeps `error` null and `result` a fresh copy of exactly the dict the single entry returns, and a failed item keeps a definite, non-empty copy of the original exception text with `result` fixed to null — the identity, digest and boundary of an unauthenticated payload never enter a result. Repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results.
51	
52	`sign_batch_receipt(items, policy, keyring, moment, issuer, version)` signs one such batch verification into a receipt that can be handed over offline, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. It takes the same `items`, `policy` and `keyring` as `verify_recovery_verdicts`, the signing `moment` and the signing `issuer` and key `version`. The batch runs through the exact `verify_recovery_verdicts` rules: batch-level faults raise directly with the same `TypeError`/`ValueError` classification, while one proof's failure is only recorded in that item's report — a failed item keeps its original status, its error text and a null `result`, and no identity or boundary is ever filled in. The receipt is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`. The payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `moment`, `policy`, `items` and `version` (integer 1): `policy` is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the canonical compact policy encoding (sites ascending, each site's versions an ascending array), and each payload item — in the original input order, never sorted, deduplicated or replaced — carries exactly `id`, `digest` (the lowercase hex SHA-256 of that item's original proof bytes) and `report` (that item's batch verification report, bound verbatim). `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback; unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`, and an empty issuer or non-positive version raises `ValueError`.
53	
54	`verify_batch_receipt(receipt, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies such a receipt entirely offline from just the receipt bytes, the expected policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It recomputes the policy digest and the signature, and checks the payload structure, the item order (each report's `id` must match its item's `id`), the item id uniqueness (a payload whose `items` repeat an `id` is rejected before any signature check), every report's shape and the moment binding, rejecting a receipt whose signing moment is later than the verification moment. The signature is checked against the key the *current* keyring binds to the payload's exact issuer and version, usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects the receipt just as it does a replay. A non-bytes receipt or any field of the wrong type — including a `bool` posing as an `int` anywhere inside the signed payload or its bound reports — raises `TypeError`; an illegal policy, keyring or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal encoding, key set, version value, digest format, duplicate item id, report shape or binding raises `InvalidBatchReceiptError` (a `ValueError` subclass); and invalid current credentials or a signature mismatch raise `AuthenticationError`. On success it returns a fresh deep copy of the payload; repeated calls return equal results that share no mutable object.
55	
56	`delegate_batch_receipt(receipt, hops, policy, keyring, moment, issuer, version, audience)` signs the next hop of a delegation chain over an already-verified base receipt, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. The base `receipt` is verified through the exact `verify_batch_receipt` rules and the existing `hops` sequence (empty for the first hop) through the full chain contract before anything is signed. The new hop's `issuer` must equal the base receipt issuer (first hop) or the previous hop's audience, its `audience` must not be the issuer itself or any identity or target domain already in the chain, and its `moment` must not be earlier than its upstream's moment. The hop is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `moment`, `audience`, `upstream` (the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the base receipt or previous hop bytes) and `version` (the integer 1), and `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback. A wrong parameter type or any field of the wrong type inside the receipt or a hop — including a `bool` posing as an `int` — raises `TypeError`; an empty issuer or audience or a non-positive version raises `ValueError`; an illegal base receipt raises `InvalidBatchReceiptError`; an illegal delegation encoding, key set, version value or chain binding raises `InvalidReceiptDelegationError` (a `ValueError` subclass); and unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`.
57	
58	`verify_batch_receipt_chain(receipt, hops, policy, keyring, moment, target)` verifies a base receipt and its whole delegation chain offline from just the bytes, the expected policy, the current keyring, the verification moment and the expected receiving domain — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. The base receipt follows the exact `verify_batch_receipt` rules; each hop is then checked in order against the canonical delegation contract (exactly `payload` and `signature`, the fixed payload fields, the `upstream` digest chaining the base receipt or previous hop bytes, the first issuer equal to the base receipt issuer, each later issuer equal to the previous hop's audience, no self-delegation, no repeated identity or target domain, and no hop moment earlier than its upstream or later than the verification moment), and each hop's signature is checked against the key the *current* keyring binds to the hop's exact issuer and version, usable both at the hop's own moment and at the verification moment with no fallback. The last hop's audience must equal `target`. A wrong parameter type or any field of the wrong type inside the receipt or a hop — including a `bool` posing as an `int` — raises `TypeError`; an empty target, an empty hop sequence or a negative moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal base receipt raises `InvalidBatchReceiptError`; an illegal delegation encoding, key set, version value or chain binding raises `InvalidReceiptDelegationError` with the first failing hop in the message; and unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials or a signature mismatch raise `AuthenticationError`. On success it returns a fresh mapping with the fixed keys `hops` (the hop payloads in chain order), `receipt` (the base receipt payload), `receiptDigest` (the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the base receipt bytes), `target` and `version` (the integer 1); repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results.
59	
60	`verify_batch_receipt_chains(items, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of those delegation chains entirely offline and adds the cross-chain delegation-fork entry point, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id`, the `receipt` bytes, a non-empty `hops` list of hop bytes and a non-empty `target` str, and reports strictly preserve input order. The whole batch structure is validated together with the shared `policy`, `keyring` and `moment` — which keep their single-chain validation and classification — before any chain is processed: container, element or field type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id, a wrong item key set or an empty hops list raises `ValueError`; only such a batch-level fault raises. Each item then runs independently through the exact `verify_batch_receipt_chain` rules, so one chain's failure never stops a later chain or changes an earlier report: a base-receipt fault is `invalid-receipt`, a delegation encoding, key-set, version-value or chain-binding fault is `invalid-delegation` and unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials or a signature mismatch are `unauthenticated`, each with the non-empty exception text and a null `result`. Successful chains are grouped by `receiptDigest` and only delegation paths under the same base receipt are ever compared; within one group, the same `upstream` digest pointing at two or more distinct legitimate next-hop audiences is a fork, while a plain prefix extension of one path is not. Every chain whose path crosses a forking edge is reclassified `conflicted`, keeping its verified single-chain result with `error` fixed to `forked-delegation`. The top-level result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `forks`, `items` and `version` (integer 1); `forks` is sorted stably by `receiptDigest` then `upstream`, each entry carrying exactly `receiptDigest`, `upstream`, ascending `audiences` and the ascending `ids` of the chains crossing that edge, and each item report carries exactly `error`, `id`, `result` (a fresh independent copy of the single-chain result when verified) and `status`. Repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results.
61	
62	`sign_receipt_fork_proof(items, policy, keyring, moment, issuer, version)` packages that fork summary into an offline-transferable signed evidence object, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. The `items`, `policy`, `keyring` and `moment` are exactly those of `verify_batch_receipt_chains`, which runs first; a proof is issued only when the resulting summary reports at least one fork (a fork-free summary raises `ValueError`). The proof is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline or any other trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`. The payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `moment`, `policy` (the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the canonical compact policy encoding), the complete `report` and `chains`, and `version` (integer 1). `chains` summarizes every input chain strictly in input order with no reordering or omission: each entry carries exactly `id`, `digest` (the SHA-256 of that chain's base receipt bytes), `target` and `hops` (the SHA-256 of each hop's complete bytes in chain order). `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback; unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`. A parameter or public field type fault raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an empty issuer, a non-positive version, a negative moment or an illegal shared policy value raises `ValueError`.
63	
64	`verify_receipt_fork_proof(proof, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies such evidence entirely offline from just the proof, the expected policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It recomputes the policy digest, validates the proof encoding, key sets, version, digests, recursive key ordering, the chain-material order and references, the complete bound chain-batch report (item count and per-position ids, result receipt digest/target/hop count, hop upstream chaining, and the forking edges and crossing chains recomputed from the bound results), rejects a signing moment later than the verification moment, and checks the HMAC against the key the *current* keyring binds to the payload's exact issuer and version, usable at the verification moment, so later revocation or expiry rejects the proof with no fallback. On success it returns a brand-new mapping with the fixed keys `chains`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `moment`, `policyDigest`, `proofDigest` (the SHA-256 of the proof bytes), `report` and `version` (integer 1). A non-bytes proof or a wrong public field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an illegal policy, keyring or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal proof encoding, key set, version, digest, ordering, reference or report binding raises `InvalidReceiptForkProofError` (a `ValueError` subclass); unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials or a signature mismatch raise `AuthenticationError`.
65	
66	`verify_receipt_fork_proofs(items, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of those proofs offline, never reading or writing a file or modifying an input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and the `proof` bytes. The batch and the shared `policy`, `keyring` and `moment` — which keep their single-proof validation and exception classification (a non-negative non-bool int) — are all validated before any proof is processed: container, element or field type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or a wrong item key set raises `ValueError`; only such a batch-level fault raises. Each proof is then verified independently through the exact `verify_receipt_fork_proof` rules, in strict input order, each selecting its key by its own exact issuer and version with no fallback: one proof's failure never stops a later proof or alters an earlier report, and a currently unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credential or a mismatched signature makes that item `unauthenticated`, an illegal encoding, key set, version, digest, ordering, reference or report binding makes it `invalid-proof`, and a passing proof is `verified`. The top-level result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items` and `version` (integer 1); each item report carries, in this key order, `error` (null exactly when verified), `id`, `result` (a fresh independent copy of the single-proof result when verified, otherwise null — the identity of an unauthenticated payload never enters a result) and `status`, each failure keeping a definite, non-empty copy of the original exception text. Repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results.
67	
68	## Multi-site fork disposition decisions
69	
70	`decide_forks(items, policy, keyring, moment, issuer, version)` turns those signed fork proofs into one multi-site disposition decision entirely offline, reading and writing no file and modifying no input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and non-empty `proof` bytes. `policy` contains exactly `action` (`"isolate"` or `"rollback"`), `base` (the existing `{"batch","sites","threshold"}` proof policy), `sites` (a non-empty map of each authorized non-empty site to its non-empty set of allowed positive key versions) and `threshold` (a positive integer no greater than the site count). Every proof is first verified through the existing receipt fork proof rules, then authorized by the exact signing site and key version with no fallback, then authenticated against the current keyring. An invalid, unauthorized or unauthenticated proof rejects only that item with one fixed reason (`invalid-proof`, `unauthorized-site`, `unauthorized-version`, `credential-unavailable`, `revoked`, `not-yet-valid`, `expired`, `bad-signature`) and never affects a later item; an identical proof digest counts once per site and extra copies are `duplicate`, while different valid proofs from the same site are a `contradiction`. The valid proofs of distinct sites must agree on every fork boundary made of the base receipt digest, the forking upstream and the target domain. A unique boundary set attested by at least the threshold of distinct sites is `accepted`, a contradiction or boundary disagreement is `conflicted`, and everything else is `insufficient`. An accepted decision recommends the policy action — isolate the deduplicated, ascending target domains, or roll back to before the fork — while every other outcome recommends `manual-review` and claims no boundary or target. The result is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object (recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved, no trailing byte) carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `action`, `boundaries`, `decisions` (sorted by site then id), `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `policyDigest` (the SHA-256 of the canonical policy), `proofs` (each proof digest in the original input order), `recommendation`, `targets` and `version` (integer 1), and the signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback. Unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired signing credentials raise `AuthenticationError`; a type fault (including a `bool` posing as an int) raises `TypeError`; an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or an illegal policy value raises `ValueError`.
71	
72	`verify_fork_decision(decision, policy, keyring, moment)` re-checks such a decision entirely offline from just the decision packet, the expected policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It validates the canonical encoding and key sets, recomputes the policy digest and the action binding, re-tallies the bound per-proof decisions (row ordering, the original-order proof digest bindings, duplicates, contradictions, cross-site boundary agreement, the threshold and the claimed boundaries, targets and recommendation) purely from the signed payload, and verifies the HMAC against the key the current keyring binds to the payload's exact issuer and version usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it. On success it returns a fresh dict keyed `action`, `boundaries`, `decisions`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `policyDigest`, `proofDigest` (the SHA-256 of the decision bytes), `proofs`, `recommendation`, `status`, `targets` and `version` (integer 1). An illegal encoding, key set, digest, ordering, reference or binding raises `InvalidForkDecisionError` (a `ValueError` subclass); unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials or a wrong signature raise `AuthenticationError`.
73	
74	`verify_fork_decisions(items, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies a non-empty batch of those decisions offline and independently, in strict input order. Each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and the `decision` bytes; the batch and the shared policy, keyring and moment are validated in full before any decision is verified, so only a batch-level fault raises (container/field faults `TypeError`; an empty list, an empty or duplicate id or a wrong item key set `ValueError`). Each decision is then reported in input order as `verified`, `invalid` or `unauthenticated` with the fixed key order `error`, `id`, `result` and `status`; a failed item keeps a definite, non-empty copy of the original exception text and a null result, and the identity of an unauthenticated payload never enters a result. Repeated calls return equal but mutually independent results. The existing proof interfaces and module commands are unchanged.

# Offline Autonomous Node Coordination

Minimal backend baseline for autonomous nodes that must keep working during long network outages and later reconcile state with explainable rules.

Requires Python 3.11 or newer and has no third-party runtime dependencies.

```bash
python -m offline_coordination status
python -m offline_coordination recovery check LEDGER [LEDGER ...]
python -m offline_coordination recovery run LEDGER [LEDGER ...] --keyring KEYRING --ticket TICKET --moment MOMENT --audit AUDIT
python -m offline_coordination recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

The baseline exposes a local status command plus offline ledger recovery operations. Persistent state is available via `offline_coordination.storage` and an append-only hash-chained audit log via `offline_coordination.audit`. Replication, conflict policies, security boundaries, observability, and network services are intentionally left for subsequent tasks.

## Ledger recovery

`offline_coordination.replication.recover_ledger(path)` settles one interrupted ledger transaction. Its `clean` result (no recovery intent) reports the SHA-256 of the current ledger bytes, lowercase hex, or `None` when the path is missing.

Two batch entry points operate on an explicit, non-empty list of distinct, non-empty ledger paths, validated in full before any file is read or modified (`TypeError` for container/element type faults, `ValueError` for an empty list, empty path or duplicate):

- `inspect_recovery(paths)` — read-only diagnostics. Each report carries `path`, `status`, `phase`, `digest`, `artifacts`, `action` and `error`: `clean` when no intent exists, `pending` with the suggested action (`rollback`/`complete`) and candidate/predecessor existence, digest-match and completeness when an intent is valid, `blocked`/`corrupt` when the intent or a necessary artifact is invalid, and `failed`/`os-error` when reading fails. Nothing is created, modified or deleted, and random artifacts are never scanned.
- `recover_many(paths)` — controlled batch recovery. Each ledger is recovered via `recover_ledger` in order; one failure never stops or rolls back the others. Successful items keep the `clean`/`rolled-back`/`completed` statuses; a `CorruptRecoveryError` becomes a `blocked`/`corrupt` item and an `OSError` a `failed`/`os-error` item, leaving enough intent and artifacts behind for an independent retry.

The module entry points `recovery check` and `recovery run` wrap these: they print exactly one line of compact UTF-8 JSON with recursively sorted keys, exit 0 when every ledger succeeds, 1 when any ledger is blocked or failed, and 2 on syntax or argument errors.

## Authorized recovery and the recovery audit

`offline_coordination.replication.recover_authorized(paths, keyring, ticket, moment, audit)` adds an authorization boundary and a durable operation audit around the same batch recovery. The ticket is one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline, space or any other byte after the closing brace; it carries exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload carries exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `nonce`, `notBefore`, `notAfter` and the ordered `paths`, and the signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload encoding, verified against the keyring (the same version/secret/validity/revocation rules as `apply_signed_remote`, keys selected by exact issuer and version). The command paths must equal the ticket paths item for item — never expanded, reordered or normalized. Unknown credentials, a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key or ticket, a path mismatch and a signature mismatch all raise `AuthenticationError` before any ledger is read, so a failed authorization creates no audit record, consumes no nonce and leaves no temporary file. An old-style ticket carrying a trailing newline (or any other non-canonical encoding) raises `ValueError`; field type faults raise `TypeError` (a `bool` never poses as `moment`); a malformed ticket key set, nonce, validity interval or signature format raises `ValueError`.

Once authorized, the batch runs in the `recover_many` order with the same per-ledger isolation and the same public item structure, and every step is recorded at the audit path as an append-only canonical JSONL hash chain, each record written, flushed and synced before the step it gates: a `batch` header on the first use of a nonce (binding the ticket digest, issuer and ordered paths), then a `before` record (original digest, phase, planned action) and an `after` record (new digest, status, failure category) per ledger. An `OSError` while reading the audit or writing, flushing or syncing a record propagates unchanged and leaves a consistent, retryable chain prefix. Re-entering with the same nonce and the same ticket reuses the recorded results and only continues the paths not yet settled — a process interrupted after a recovery but before its result record is completed from the recorded action and digests, without repeating side effects. The same nonce bound to a different ticket raises `ReplayError` (a `ValueError`) without modifying any file; a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError` (a `ValueError`).

`export_recovery_audit(path, after=0, limit=100)` pages the chain read-only (`after`/`complete`/`next`/`records`), validating the whole chain and treating a missing audit as an empty chain. The module entry point `recovery run` requires the four explicit materials `--keyring`, `--ticket`, `--moment` and `--audit` and exits 0 on success, 1 on ledger failures and 2 on authorization or argument errors; `recovery audit AUDIT [--after N] [--limit N]` prints one page of the chain.

`export_recovery_checkpoint(audit, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` adds an offline signature anchor that a later full-history replacement cannot recompute. It reads and validates the whole chain read-only and returns `bytes`: one compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing newline or any other trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`. The payload binds exactly `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `lastSeq`, `moment`, `tail` and `version` (integer 1) — `lastSeq` is the last chain seq (0 for a missing audit) and `tail` the last record hash (the zero hash for an empty chain). `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key the keyring binds to the exact issuer and version, with no fallback; unknown credentials and a revoked, not-yet-valid or expired key raise `AuthenticationError`, a corrupt chain raises `CorruptRecoveryAuditError`, and an `OSError` while reading propagates unchanged.

`verify_recovery_page(checkpoint, page, keyring, moment, cursor=None)` verifies a page dict against the checkpoint entirely offline — no file is read and no argument is modified. The checkpoint is parsed and its HMAC verified against the current keyring (exact issuer/version, usable at `moment`, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it); the bound `moment` is part of the signed payload itself. The first call passes no cursor and the page's `after` must be zero; later calls pass `{"digest", "next", "tail"}` built from the previous result, so `after` must equal the cursor `next`, the first record must chain to the cursor `tail`, and the cursor `digest` must equal this checkpoint's SHA-256 digest — a cursor can never resume another checkpoint. Each page's records must be contiguous from `after + 1` (no empty page, gap, reordering, duplicate or predecessor mismatch before the signed end), hash-correct within the page and across the paging boundary, and verification never crosses the signed `lastSeq`. The result carries `digest`, `lastSeq`, `status` and `tail`: reaching the signed tail is `verified`, every earlier page `continue`. An empty checkpoint accepts only an empty page starting at zero and directly reports seq 0, the zero hash and `verified`. Parameter or field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); keyring structure or format faults raise `ValueError`; checkpoint faults raise `InvalidRecoveryCheckpointError` and page or cursor faults raise `InvalidRecoveryPageError`, both `ValueError` subclasses.

`verify_recovery_checkpoints(items, keyring, moment)` verifies a whole batch of checkpoints offline and never reads a file. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id`, the `checkpoint` bytes and the non-empty `pages` list holding that checkpoint's paging dicts in export order. The batch is validated in full before any item is verified — container, field or element type faults raise `TypeError` and an empty list, an empty or duplicate id, a wrong item key set or an empty page list raises `ValueError` (keyring and `moment`, a non-negative non-bool int, keep their usual classification). Each item is then handled in input order and in isolation: its pages are walked from a zero cursor through the exact `verify_recovery_page` rules, each cursor bound to the same checkpoint digest and the previous page's chain tail; keys are selected by the checkpoint's own exact issuer and version with no fallback, so checkpoints signed before and after a key rotation verify independently in one batch while the keyring retains both versions. Pages that reach the signed `lastSeq` must end there (any further page is a page fault); pages exhausted earlier are `incomplete` and keep the verified boundary. The result is a fresh dict with the fixed keys `items`, `version` (integer 1); each item report carries `id`, the checkpoint `digest`, the signed `issuer` and `keyVersion` (both null when the checkpoint does not parse), the verified `boundary` (`{"lastSeq","tail"}`, null when nothing was verified), a `status` of `verified`, `incomplete`, `invalid-checkpoint`, `invalid-page` or `unauthenticated`, and an `error` message (null exactly when verified). Only a batch-level or keyring-level fault raises — one item's failure never stops the later items, and no input is modified.

`adjudicate_recovery(items, policy, keyring, moment)` aggregates those per-site verifications into one offline verdict, reading no file and modifying no input. `items` is a non-empty list; each item contains exactly a non-empty, batch-unique `id` and `attestation` bytes. An attestation is a compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `site`, `keyVersion` and `result` with no extra fields, where `result` has the single-item batch verification shape (`boundary`, `digest`, `error`, `id`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `status`). Every legal single-item result is accepted: a `verified` result always carries identity, a positive key version and a boundary, while a non-verified result may carry a null issuer/keyVersion (when the checkpoint did not parse) or a null boundary — its identity, digest, boundary and status are preserved — and only a `verified` result may count. `policy` is `{"batch", "sites", "threshold"}`: the authorized batch id, a positive threshold no greater than the site count, and a non-empty map of each authorized site to its non-empty set of allowed positive key versions; `keyring` and `moment` keep their existing structure, validity and revocation rules. The signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key selected by the exact site and version, with no fallback.

A batch or identity that is not authorized, unavailable/revoked/not-yet-valid/expired credentials, a wrong signature or a non-verified result each reject the packet with a fixed reason (`unauthorized-batch`, `unauthorized-site`, `unauthorized-version`, `credential-unavailable`, `revoked`, `not-yet-valid`, `expired`, `bad-signature`, `not-verified`) and never count; one packet with illegal encoding, key sets or fields is rejected alone as `invalid-attestation` without blocking the others. For one site an identical valid packet — the complete embedded result equal on every field — counts once and extra copies are `duplicate`; any different valid result (even one sharing digest and boundary) is a self-`contradiction`. Valid packets from different sites must agree on both digest and boundary — any disagreement is a fork a majority cannot outvote. The return is one canonical compact JSON object with the top-level keys `boundary`, `digest`, `items`, `status`, `threshold` and `version` (integer 1), no trailing byte: any contradiction or cross-site fork is `conflicted` with a null digest and boundary; a unique agreed result attested by at least the threshold of distinct sites is `accepted`; everything else is `insufficient`. Every packet stays in `items` — sorted stably by site then id — with its identity, conclusion (`valid`/`invalid`/`duplicate`/`contradiction`), fixed reason (null only for valid) and boundary, and the verdict does not depend on input order. Parameter, container or public field type faults raise `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); an empty list, duplicate id or illegal threshold, site or version rule raises `ValueError`.

`export_recovery_verdict(verdict, policy, keyring, issuer, version, moment)` signs that aggregate verdict for offline handover, reading and writing no file. It takes the canonical compact verdict bytes `adjudicate_recovery` returned, the same policy, a keyring, the signing issuer, key version and moment. It returns one canonical compact UTF-8 JSON object with recursively sorted keys, non-ASCII preserved and no trailing byte, carrying exactly `payload` and `signature`; the payload binds exactly `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest` and the complete `verdict`. The policy is canonicalized — sites in ascending order and each site's versions as an ascending array, all keys recursively sorted into compact UTF-8 — and `policyDigest` is its SHA-256; `signature` is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical compact payload bytes under the key bound to the exact issuer and version with no fallback. Unknown, revoked, not-yet-valid or expired credentials raise `AuthenticationError`. A non-bytes verdict or a wrong field type raises `TypeError` (a bool never poses as an int); a bad issuer, version or moment raises `ValueError`; an illegal verdict raises `InvalidRecoveryVerdictError`.

`verify_recovery_verdict(proof, policy, keyring, moment)` verifies such a handover proof entirely offline from just the proof, the policy, the current keyring and the verification moment — no file is read or written and no argument is modified. It recomputes the two digests, checks the batch, threshold, signing moment, proof/verdict structure and digest bindings, and re-checks the credentials against the current keyring (exact issuer/version usable at the verification moment, so a later revocation or expiry rejects it). It returns a fresh dict keyed `batch`, `issuer`, `keyVersion`, `signedAt`, `policyDigest`, `verdictDigest`, `status`, `digest`, `boundary`, `items` and `version` (integer 1). 1	"""Read-only audit replication batches.
2	
3	A batch is a single UTF-8 compact JSON object (non-ASCII preserved, no
4	whitespace) terminated by exactly one ``\\n``::
5	
6	    {"after":...,"complete":...,"next":...,"records":[...],"version":1}
7	
8	The top-level keys are fixed in the order ``after``, ``complete``,
9	``next``, ``records``, ``version`` and ``version`` is always the integer
10	1.  ``after`` echoes the request's ``after`` argument.  ``records`` holds
11	up to ``limit`` (at most 1000) audit records whose ``seq`` is greater
12	than ``after``, in audit order, each preserving the audit record key
13	order ``detail, hash, kind, prev, seq, source`` and its original values.
14	``next`` is the seq of the last record in the batch, or ``after`` itself
15	when the batch is empty; ``complete`` is true when no record follows the
16	batch, and an empty ``records`` list is only valid when ``complete`` is
17	true.  Batches are generated solely through :func:`audit.read`, so the
18	audit log is never modified and :class:`~offline_coordination.audit.
19	CorruptAuditError` and :class:`OSError` propagate unchanged.
20	
21	:func:`import_batch` validates a batch against this byte contract and
22	appends its records to the local log.  It returns a dict with the fixed
23	key order ``need``, ``next``, ``status``.  When the batch starts beyond
24	the local log (``after`` greater than the local last seq ``L``) nothing is
25	written and ``status`` is ``"missing"`` with ``need`` holding the gap
26	``[L + 1, after]`` and ``next`` set to ``L``.  Otherwise records already
27	present locally must match field by field (a mismatch raises
28	:class:`ValueError`); the matching prefix is skipped idempotently and
29	only the contiguous suffix past ``L`` is appended, linked to the local
30	last hash.  ``need`` is then ``None``, ``next`` is ``max(L, batch.next)``
31	and ``status`` is ``"applied"`` when records were appended, else
32	``"duplicate"``.  Any failure leaves the log untouched.
33	
34	Batches are checked only against the byte contract: canonical encoding, key
35	order, the seq/prev/hash chain and the stored values.  Value-domain rules
36	enforced by :func:`audit.append` on event input (the kind enum, non-empty
37	string fields) are *not* re-enforced here, so every log :func:`audit.read`
38	accepts round-trips through :func:`export_batch`/:func:`import_batch`.  The
39	append itself is atomic: when the write, flush or fsync step raises
40	:class:`OSError` the error propagates unchanged and the log is left
41	byte-identical to its pre-call state (still missing when it was missing).
42	
43	:func:`apply_remote` persists remote state applications in a version-1
44	*ledger*: one UTF-8 compact JSON object (keys sorted lexicographically,
45	exactly one trailing ``\\n``) with the top-level keys ``audit``,
46	``requests``, ``state`` and ``version`` (``version`` is the integer 1).
47	``state`` holds the current :mod:`~offline_coordination.merge` state,
48	``requests`` binds each accepted request id to the digest of its request,
49	and ``audit`` lists one entry per successful application in order; each
50	entry carries ``after``/``before`` state digests, the request ``id`` and
51	``source`` and a contiguous ``seq`` starting at 1, every entry after the
52	first chaining its ``before`` to the previous entry's ``after`` and the
53	last ``after`` hashing the stored state.  A missing ledger stands for the
54	request's ``base`` state with empty indexes; any existing file that fails
55	the byte, structure, state or index rules is rejected with
56	:class:`ValueError` and left untouched.
57	
58	Replaying a request whose ``id`` is already bound to exactly the same
59	request digest always yields ``duplicate`` from the saved binding alone,
60	immediately or after other commits: one item per remote record in
61	ascending key order, each already duplicate with an empty ``need`` map,
62	and no receipt; the ledger is never read for modification on a replay.
63	A bound ``id`` presented with a different request raises
64	:class:`ValueError`.  Every successful commit is one durable transaction:
65	write, flush, file sync, replacement and directory sync all lie inside
66	its boundary, and an :class:`OSError` at any stage propagates unchanged
67	with the file system restored to its pre-call state.
68	
69	Each commit is additionally backed by a *recovery intent* so a crash of
70	the committing process itself can be reconciled later, across processes.
71	Before anything is replaced, the commit publishes an intent at ``path +
72	".txn"``: one UTF-8 compact JSON object (keys recursively sorted,
73	exactly one trailing ``\n``) recording only ``version`` (the integer 1),
74	``phase``, the lowercase hex SHA-256 digests of the new and old ledger
75	bytes (``newDigest``/``oldDigest``) and the safe base names of the
76	candidate and predecessor transaction files, all confined to the
77	ledger's own directory; when the ledger did not exist, ``oldDigest`` and
78	``predecessor`` are both ``null``.  The intent starts in phase
79	``prepared`` and is republished as ``installed`` only after the new
80	ledger has replaced the old one and the directory has synced; the
81	intent's own creation and phase change each sync the file and the
82	directory.  A crash before the ``installed`` intent is durable leaves
83	the commit unconfirmed: :func:`recover_ledger` keeps or restores the old
84	bytes (byte-for-byte, and missing again when the path was missing) and
85	deletes the referenced candidate.  A crash afterwards lets
86	:func:`recover_ledger` verify the new bytes against ``newDigest`` and
87	finish the cleanup.  Only files the intent references are removed, the
88	intent itself is deleted last and the directory is synced, and a
89	repeated call reports ``clean`` without scanning random artifacts.
90	
91	:func:`recover_ledger` returns a fresh dict with the key order
92	``digest``, ``status``: ``clean`` when no intent exists, ``rolled-back``
93	or ``completed`` after a recovery, with ``digest`` holding the digest of
94	the resulting ledger bytes (``None`` when the path is missing).  A
95	``path`` that is not a str raises :class:`TypeError`; an intent that
96	fails to parse, or whose fields, phase, names, digests or necessary
97	artifacts are invalid, raises :class:`CorruptRecoveryError` (a
98	:class:`ValueError`) without touching the ledger or any unrelated file;
99	an :class:`OSError` while reading, replacing, deleting or syncing
100	propagates unchanged with enough intent and artifacts left for a retry.
101	The ledger write entry points run this recovery automatically after
102	their input validation, before the ledger is read.
103	
104	:func:`inspect_recovery` diagnoses an explicit, non-empty list of ledger
105	paths without modifying anything: only each listed ledger, its intent
106	and the artifacts the intent references are read.  Each report carries
107	``path``, ``status``, ``phase``, ``digest``, ``artifacts``, ``action``
108	and ``error`` -- ``clean`` with a null phase and action when no intent
109	exists (the digest still summarizes the ledger bytes, or is null when
110	the path is missing), ``pending`` with the intent's phase and the
111	suggested action (``rollback``/``complete``) plus the candidate and
112	predecessor existence, digest match and completeness when an intent is
113	valid, ``blocked``/``corrupt`` when the intent or a necessary artifact
114	is invalid, and ``failed``/``os-error`` when reading fails.
115	:func:`recover_many` is the controlled batch form of
116	:func:`recover_ledger` over the same kind of list: every path is
117	recovered in order, one ledger's failure never stops or rolls back the
118	others, a :class:`CorruptRecoveryError` becomes a ``blocked``/``corrupt``
119	item and an :class:`OSError` a ``failed``/``os-error`` item, and failed
120	ledgers keep their intent and artifacts so a re-run retries them
121	independently.  Both validate the whole list (a non-empty list of
122	non-empty, distinct strings) before any file is read or modified.
123	
124	:func:`apply_signed_remote` adds an offline-verifiable authentication
125	boundary in front of the same application flow.  It receives the ledger
126	path, a keyring, an envelope and the current moment.  The envelope
127	carries exactly ``node``, ``keyVersion``, ``request`` and ``signature``;
128	the request follows the :func:`apply_remote` contract and its ``source``
129	must equal the envelope's ``node``.  The keyring maps node names to
130	credential entries, each holding exactly ``version`` (a positive integer,
131	unique per node), ``secret`` (64 lowercase hex characters decoding to the
132	32-byte HMAC key), ``notBefore``/``notAfter`` (non-negative integers
133	bounding the validity period, both bounds inclusive) and ``revoked``.
134	The signed payload is the canonical compact UTF-8 JSON encoding of
135	``node``, ``keyVersion`` and ``request`` with every object key
136	recursively sorted lexicographically and non-ASCII preserved; the
137	signature is the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 computed with the selected key
138	and compared in constant time.  Keys are selected by exact node and
139	version with no fallback: unknown credentials, a revoked, not-yet-valid
140	or expired key, a source/node identity mismatch and a signature mismatch
141	all raise :class:`AuthenticationError` (a :class:`ValueError`) before the
142	ledger is ever read, so a failed verification creates no file.  Replays
143	are authenticated against the *current* keyring, so a later revocation or
144	expiry cannot be bypassed through a historical request binding.  Audit
145	entries committed through :func:`apply_signed_remote` record the verified
146	credentials under ``auth``; entries without ``auth`` remain readable and
147	:func:`apply_remote` keeps its public behaviour and ledger format.
148	
149	:func:`export_proof` and :func:`verify_proof` add offline audit-proof
150	exchange over the same ledger.  A proof is one version-1 UTF-8 compact
151	JSON object -- every object key recursively sorted lexicographically,
152	non-ASCII preserved, exactly one trailing ``\\n`` -- with the top-level
153	keys ``digest``, ``endSeq``, ``entries``, ``firstBefore``, ``lastAfter``,
154	``startSeq`` and ``version``.  ``startSeq``/``endSeq`` name the covered
155	audit range, ``firstBefore`` is the state digest before the first covered
156	entry and ``lastAfter`` the state digest after the last one; ``entries``
157	hold the ledger entries in range unchanged, each carrying ``after``/
158	``before`` state digests, ``id``, ``seq`` and ``source`` with the optional
159	``auth`` binding.  ``digest`` is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of the compact
160	canonical encoding (with no trailing newline) of the proof object with
161	the ``digest`` key itself removed.  :func:`verify_proof` is purely
162	offline: it reads neither the ledger nor the keyring.
163	
164	:func:`compare_proofs` relates two proofs offline, on top of that same
165	purely local verification.  Both arguments are :class:`bytes`; they are
166	first independently checked against the exact :func:`verify_proof`
167	contract, so a non-bytes argument raises :class:`TypeError` and either
168	proof being invalid raises :class:`InvalidProofError` before any
169	comparison.  The ledger, the keyring and the filesystem are never read
170	and neither input is modified.  The result is one version-1 UTF-8
171	compact JSON object -- every object key sorted lexicographically,
172	non-ASCII preserved, exactly one trailing ``\\n`` -- with the fixed
173	top-level keys ``common``, ``conflictSeq``, ``left``, ``overlap``,
174	``relation``, ``right`` and ``version`` (``version`` is the integer 1).
175	``left``/``right`` each carry the proof ``digest`` and its
176	``startSeq``/``endSeq``.  ``overlap`` is the closed shared seq interval
177	``[start, end]`` or ``null`` when the two ranges are disjoint; disjoint
178	ranges never raise and keep both sides' ranges.  With an overlap, the
179	complete entries at every shared seq are compared in ascending seq
180	order -- boundary and proof digests alone are never enough.  If every
181	shared entry matches, ``relation`` is ``"same"`` (identical ranges),
182	``"left-prefix"``/``"right-prefix"`` (same start and the shorter side
183	matches in full, named for the shorter side) or ``"overlap"``
184	otherwise; ``common`` then names the last shared boundary as
185	``{"after", "seq"}`` -- the last common entry's seq and after digest.
186	The first shared seq whose complete entry differs makes ``relation``
187	``"fork"`` with ``conflictSeq`` that earliest seq (never skipped past);
188	``common`` is the last equal entry when an equal entry precedes it, the
189	prior boundary ``{"after", "seq"}`` when the first shared entry already
190	conflicts but its ``before`` digests agree (its seq may be 0), and
191	``null`` when those ``before`` digests differ.  ``conflictSeq`` is
192	``null`` for every non-fork relation.  The bytes are deterministic for
193	equal inputs; swapping the inputs only exchanges ``left``/``right`` and
194	mirrors the prefix direction.
195	
196	:func:`plan_merge` turns that read-only comparison into a read-only merge
197	plan.  It takes both proof byte strings and a conflict ``policy`` --
198	``"left"``, ``"right"`` or ``"manual"``; any other value raises
199	:class:`ValueError` -- and validates every argument type before parsing
200	either proof, so a malformed proof never masks a :class:`TypeError` and an
201	invalid proof still raises :class:`InvalidProofError`.  Disjoint ranges,
202	or a fork whose common boundary cannot be confirmed, raise
203	:class:`ValueError` instead of producing a speculative plan.  Only
204	complete entries strictly after the common boundary become steps: an

206	fork accepts the selected side's tail (``selected``) and rejects the
207	other (``rejected``), while ``manual`` marks both tails ``manual`` and
208	references them from ``unresolved``.  The plan is one version-1 UTF-8
209	compact JSON object -- keys recursively sorted, non-ASCII preserved,
210	exactly one trailing ``\\n`` -- with the top-level keys ``common``,
211	``left``, ``policy``, ``relation``, ``right``, ``steps``, ``unresolved``
212	and ``version``; steps carry the original entries unchanged and are
213	ordered by ascending seq with the left side first on ties.  The plan is
214	byte-stable for equal inputs, mirrors left/right when the proofs are
215	swapped together with a ``left``/``right`` policy, and never touches the
216	filesystem or the inputs.
217	
218	:func:`resolve_merge` closes a ``manual`` plan read-only.  It takes the
219	plan byte string, the same two proofs and a list of decisions; only a
220	``manual`` plan produced by :func:`plan_merge` for exactly those proofs
221	may be resolved -- a plan from any other policy is a structurally valid
222	version-1 plan whose steps differ from the regenerated manual plan and
223	is therefore rejected as stale before any decision is considered.
224	A structurally invalid plan (encoding, duplicate keys, version-1
225	structure) raises :class:`InvalidPlanError`; a structurally valid plan
226	that is not byte-for-byte the manual plan regenerated from the proofs
227	(digest, relation, common boundary, side summaries, steps or unresolved
228	references) raises :class:`StalePlanError`; both are
229	:class:`ValueError` subclasses.  Each decision carries only ``side``,
230	``seq`` and ``action`` (``"accept"`` or ``"reject"``), resolving one
231	unresolved reference; missing, duplicate, extra or out-of-range
232	references and illegal choices raise :class:`InvalidResolutionError`

234	the common boundary -- at most one accepted side per seq, no acceptance
235	past a rejected seq, an unbroken seq and digest chain.  The result is
236	one version-1 compact JSON object with the top-level keys ``common``,
237	``left``, ``planDigest``, ``relation``, ``right``, ``steps``,
238	``unresolved`` and ``version``; manual steps become
239	``accept``/``reject`` with the fixed reasons ``manual-accepted``/
240	``manual-rejected``, non-manual steps, carried audit entries and ``auth``

244	and never touches the filesystem or the inputs.
245	
246	:func:`commit_resolution` is the write entry point that lands a manual
247	resolution in the ledger.  It takes the ledger path, the canonical

batch, and an empty ``records`` list is only valid when ``complete`` is
